To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

genetic factors control sensitivity to DES-induced atrophy of the rat thymus, that the genetic factors are distinct from factors controlling the effects of estrogen on pituitary growth, and that the genetic factors overlap with loci controlling sensitivity to radiation-induced apoptosis and susceptibility to autoimmune diseases in rodents.
we have mapped three genetic determinants of diethylstilbesterol-induced thymic apoptosis on rat chromosomes 2 and 10.
genetic factors that determine sensitivity to diethylstilbesterol-induced thymic involution in rats also determine susceptibility to a variety radiation-induced and autoimmune diseases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the genetic determinants of the sensitivity of the BN strain of rats to estrogen-induced thymi atrophy and the effects of estrogen on thymic cell turnover.
the identification and characterization of genetic determinants of estrogen-induced thymocyte atrophy in rats.
the genetic control of the sensitivity of the thymus to estrogenic compounds and its relationship to the maintenance of thymic homeostasis and immune function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
genetic determinants of estrogen sensitivity control the effects of estrogen on thymic atrophies and immune function.

the genetic determinants of estrogen-induced thymocyte atrophy are distinct but closely linked to loci that control the effects on pituitary and body mass and are closely linked to locii that control the maintenance of thymocytes.
the sensitivity of the Brown Norway (Bn) rat to diethylstilbesterol (DES)-induced thymic atropy is a polygenic trait.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Esta loci control the ability to maintain a normal thymic environment for thymocyte development.
the Esta loci are likely to be involved in the control of thymocyte proliferation and/or survival.

genetic factors controlling sensitivity to DES-induced atrophy of thymic tissue in the Brown Norway (Bn) rat are distinct from those controlling DES-induced inhibition of growth or pituitary tumorgenesis in this strain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic determinants of DES-induced thymus atrophy are distinct genetic loci from those that control DES-induced pituitary tumours and DES-induced growth suppression.
there may be a common genetic determinant of sensitivity to DES and radiation-induced thymic involution.
